feedback: If a learner names the tile 1/7 (3 columns + 4 rows), pause and count the tiles in one unit square out loud together: 3 across, 4 down — the grid makes 12 tiles, not 7. The number of columns and the number of rows multiply (3 × 4 = 12); they do not add.
If a learner reports the edge of the shaded rectangle instead of the interior, distinguish 'how far around' from 'how much surface': point to and count the filling tiles, not the boundary.

If a learner is unsettled that 1/2 is smaller than both 2/3 and 3/4, show that taking a fraction (less than 1) OF another fraction gives a part of a part, so here it is smaller than either factor — the whole unit square is the reference, and the shaded block spans 2/3 of the width and 3/4 of the height, so it covers only half the whole square. (This 'smaller than both' result holds because both side lengths are less than 1; a mixed-number side such as 1 1/2 can give a larger product.)
Confirm success when the learner links 3×4 to the tile count/denominator and 2×3 to the shaded count/numerator, keeping the unit square as the named whole throughout.
activities.intendedInsight: Cutting the unit square in two directions redefines the unit into b×d equal tiles (so denominators multiply) and the shaded a×c block gives the numerator — this is why (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, and why the product can be smaller than both sides when both sides are less than 1.
learnerActions: Start from one whole unit square. Partition it in two directions — cut it into 3 columns one way and 4 rows the other way — to model 2/3 × 3/4.
Count the small tiles that appear in the whole unit square (3 across × 4 down = 12) and name the value of ONE tile: 1/12 of the unit square.
Shade the 2-by-3 corner block (2 of the 3 columns, 3 of the 4 rows) and count the shaded tiles: 2×3 = 6, so 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2.
Compare the shaded rectangle against the whole unit square and confirm it is exactly half of it — an area smaller than either side length (because each side is less than 1).
Say aloud which number in the picture gives the denominator (3×4 = 12 tiles per unit) and which gives the numerator (2×3 = 6 shaded tiles).
activities.title: Build the area and watch the tiles appear

feedback: If the drawing has parallel strips (cut in one direction only), prompt: 'the OTHER side also has to be cut — how many pieces that way?' Have the learner lay the second set of cuts and re-count the grid before reading the area.
If the learner writes 4/5 or 1/2 as the answer, point back to the tile value: there are 10 tiles per unit, so each is 1/10 and 4 of them is 4/10 = 2/5.
For the 1 1/2 × 2/3 extension, check that the grid spans a full unit plus a half-unit wide (and 2/3 tall), so tiles are counted across both unit squares; with tiles of 1/6 the area comes to 6/6 = 1.

A produce-mode on a two-way tiler (blank grid; learner builds the product; it checks tile worth and shaded count) or offline drawing both work; the point is that the learner constructs the two cuts, not selects from options.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing both partitions yourself — not just one — is what shows you own the idea that two cuts redefine the unit; the model scales to mixed numbers by tiling more than one unit square.
learnerActions: On a blank unit square, DRAW a rectangle showing 1/2 × 4/5: choose the two cuts yourself — partition into 2 one way and 5 the other way.
Name what one tile is worth (1/10) and explain why: 2×5 = 10 tiles fill the unit.
Shade a 1-by-4 block (4 tiles) and read the area: 4/10 = 2/5.
Say which cuts produced the 10 and which shaded tiles produced the 4, pointing to each number in your own drawing.

Extend the model: tile across more than one unit square to find the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 (here the product is 1, larger than the 2/3 side — a useful check that the 'smaller than both' intuition only applies when both sides are less than 1).
activities.title: Produce your own diagram for a fresh product
